questions.stem: What are the four bases found in DNA?

options.text: Adenine, Uracil, Guanine, Cytosine
Adenine, Thymine, Guanine, Cytosine
Adenine, Thymine, Guanine, Uridine
Alanine, Thymine, Glycine, Cysteine

questions.explanation: The four bases in DNA are Adenine (A), Thymine (T), Guanine (G), and Cytosine (C). In RNA, Thymine is replaced by Uracil (U). Option D lists amino acids, not DNA bases — a common confusion.

questions.stem: What are the three components of a DNA nucleotide?

options.text: Phosphate group, ribose sugar, nitrogenous base
Phosphate group, deoxyribose sugar, nitrogenous base
Amino acid, phosphate group, sugar
Fatty acid, sugar, base

questions.explanation: A DNA nucleotide contains a phosphate group, a deoxyribose sugar, and a nitrogenous base. RNA nucleotides contain ribose sugar instead of deoxyribose. The 'deoxy' in deoxyribose means it has one fewer oxygen atom than ribose.

questions.stem: What type of bond holds the two complementary strands of DNA together?

options.text: Covalent bonds between the bases
Ionic bonds between the sugars
Hydrogen bonds between complementary base pairs
Peptide bonds between the nucleotides

questions.explanation: Hydrogen bonds form between complementary base pairs (A-T with 2 hydrogen bonds, G-C with 3 hydrogen bonds), holding the two DNA strands together. Phosphodiester bonds (covalent) hold the nucleotides within each strand. The hydrogen bonds are weak individually but collectively keep the double helix stable while allowing the strands to separate during replication and transcription.

questions.stem: According to Chargaff's rules, if a DNA sample contains 30% adenine, what percentage of the bases is cytosine?
questions.explanation: Chargaff's rules state that in double-stranded DNA, A = T and G = C. If A = 30%, then T = 30%, so A + T = 60%. The remaining 40% is split equally between G and C, so C = 20%. These rules apply to double-stranded DNA but NOT to single-stranded RNA.

questions.stem: Do Chargaff's rules (A=T, G=C) apply to single-stranded RNA?

options.text: Yes — the rules apply to all nucleic acids
No — Chargaff's rules only apply to double-stranded DNA, because RNA is single-stranded and does not have complementary base pairing along its length
Yes — but uracil replaces thymine, so A=U and G=C
No — because RNA does not contain bases

questions.explanation: Chargaff's rules (A=T, G=C) apply only to double-stranded DNA, where each base on one strand is paired with its complement on the other. Single-stranded RNA does not have a complementary strand along its entire length, so there is no requirement for A to equal U or G to equal C.

questions.stem: What is a gene?

options.text: An entire chromosome
A sequence of DNA bases that codes for a specific polypeptide (protein)
A single nucleotide
The entire DNA molecule in a cell

questions.explanation: A gene is a section of DNA that contains the sequence of bases coding for a specific polypeptide (protein). Genes are located on chromosomes. A chromosome contains many genes, and the complete set of genes in an organism is called its genome.

questions.stem: Do all cells in the human body contain the same genes?

options.text: No — each cell type only has the genes it needs
Yes — all cells contain the same genes, but different genes are expressed in different cell types
No — genes are only present in reproductive cells
Yes — and all genes are active in every cell

questions.explanation: Almost all cells in the body contain the same complete set of genes (the genome). However, different cell types express different genes — this is called differential gene expression. For example, only red blood cell precursors express the gene for haemoglobin. This is how one genome produces many different cell types.

questions.stem: What is DNA replication?

options.text: The process of making mRNA from DNA
The process of making an exact copy of a DNA molecule before cell division
The process of making proteins from mRNA
The process of breaking down DNA for recycling

questions.explanation: DNA replication is the process of producing two identical copies of a DNA molecule. It occurs during the S phase of interphase, before cell division. This ensures each daughter cell receives a complete copy of the genetic information. Replication is semi-conservative — each new molecule contains one old strand and one new strand.

questions.stem: What does 'semi-conservative' mean in the context of DNA replication?

options.text: Half the DNA is destroyed during replication
Each new DNA molecule contains one original (parent) strand and one newly synthesised strand
Only half the genes are copied
The DNA is only partially unwound

questions.explanation: Semi-conservative replication means each new DNA molecule consists of one original (parent) strand and one newly synthesised strand. This was demonstrated by the Meselson-Stahl experiment using heavy nitrogen (¹⁵N). 'Semi' means half — half the original molecule is conserved in each new molecule.

questions.stem: What is the role of DNA helicase in DNA replication?

options.text: It adds new nucleotides to the growing strand
It joins Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand
It unwinds the double helix and breaks the hydrogen bonds between complementary base pairs
It proofreads the new DNA strand for errors

questions.explanation: DNA helicase unwinds the DNA double helix and breaks the hydrogen bonds between complementary base pairs, separating the two strands. This creates a replication fork where new nucleotides can be added. DNA polymerase then adds complementary nucleotides to each template strand.

questions.stem: What is the role of DNA polymerase in DNA replication?

options.text: It unwinds the DNA double helix
It adds free nucleotides to the template strand, forming phosphodiester bonds
It breaks down the old DNA strand
It converts RNA into DNA

questions.explanation: DNA polymerase adds free DNA nucleotides that are complementary to the template strand. It forms phosphodiester bonds between adjacent nucleotides, building the new strand in the 5' to 3' direction. It can also proofread and correct errors.

questions.stem: Where does transcription take place in a eukaryotic cell?

options.text: In the cytoplasm
In the nucleus
On the ribosomes
In the mitochondria only

questions.explanation: Transcription takes place in the nucleus, where the DNA is located. RNA polymerase reads the template strand of DNA and produces a complementary mRNA molecule. The mRNA then leaves the nucleus through nuclear pores and travels to ribosomes in the cytoplasm for translation.

questions.stem: Where does translation take place?

options.text: In the nucleus
In the mitochondria
On ribosomes in the cytoplasm (or on the rough ER)
In the Golgi apparatus

questions.explanation: Translation occurs on ribosomes, which can be free in the cytoplasm or attached to the rough endoplasmic reticulum. The ribosome reads the mRNA codons and assembles amino acids (brought by tRNA) into a polypeptide chain.

questions.stem: Which strand of DNA is used as a template during transcription?

options.text: The coding (sense) strand
Both strands simultaneously
The template (antisense) strand, read in the 3' to 5' direction
Neither — RNA is made from amino acids, not DNA

questions.explanation: During transcription, RNA polymerase reads the template (antisense) strand in the 3' to 5' direction and builds the mRNA in the 5' to 3' direction. The resulting mRNA sequence is complementary to the template strand and matches the coding (sense) strand (except U replaces T).

questions.stem: If the DNA template strand reads 3'-TACGGA-5', what is the mRNA sequence?

options.text: 3'-TACGGA-5'
5'-AUGCCU-3'
5'-ATGCCT-3'
3'-UACGGA-5'

questions.explanation: mRNA is built complementary to the template strand and in the antiparallel direction: T→A, A→U, C→G, G→C, G→C, A→U. So the mRNA is 5'-AUGCCU-3'. Remember that RNA uses uracil (U) instead of thymine (T), and the mRNA runs in the 5' to 3' direction.

questions.stem: What is a codon?

options.text: A sequence of two bases on mRNA that codes for an amino acid
A sequence of three bases on mRNA that codes for a specific amino acid
A sequence of three bases on tRNA
A single base on DNA

questions.explanation: A codon is a sequence of three consecutive bases (triplet) on mRNA that codes for one specific amino acid. There are 64 possible codons: 61 code for amino acids and 3 are stop codons. The codon on mRNA pairs with the complementary anticodon on tRNA during translation.

questions.stem: What is an anticodon?

options.text: A sequence of three bases on mRNA
A sequence of three bases on DNA
A sequence of three bases on tRNA that is complementary to an mRNA codon
The stop signal at the end of a gene

questions.explanation: An anticodon is a triplet of bases on tRNA that is complementary (and antiparallel) to a specific codon on mRNA. During translation, the anticodon on tRNA base-pairs with the codon on mRNA, ensuring the correct amino acid is added to the growing polypeptide chain.

questions.stem: What is the role of tRNA in translation?

options.text: To carry the genetic code from the nucleus to the ribosome
To carry specific amino acids to the ribosome and match them to the correct mRNA codon via its anticodon
To make up the structure of the ribosome
To synthesise amino acids from nucleotides

questions.explanation: tRNA (transfer RNA) carries specific amino acids to the ribosome during translation. Each tRNA has an anticodon that binds to the complementary codon on mRNA, and an amino acid attachment site at the other end. This ensures amino acids are assembled in the correct order to form the polypeptide.

questions.stem: What does 'degenerate' (or 'redundant') mean when describing the genetic code?

options.text: The code is full of errors
Most amino acids are coded for by more than one codon
Each codon codes for multiple different amino acids
The code is different in every organism

questions.explanation: The genetic code is degenerate (redundant) because most amino acids are coded for by more than one codon. For example, leucine is coded by six different codons. There are 64 codons but only 20 amino acids, so multiple codons must code for the same amino acid. This provides some protection against mutations.

questions.stem: Does translation create new amino acids?

options.text: Yes — amino acids are synthesised at the ribosome
No — translation assembles existing free amino acids into a polypeptide chain in the correct sequence
Yes — but only the essential amino acids
No — amino acids come from DNA directly

questions.explanation: Translation does NOT create amino acids. It assembles existing free amino acids (brought by tRNA) into a polypeptide chain in the order specified by the mRNA codons. Amino acids are obtained from the diet or synthesised in the body through other metabolic pathways, not at the ribosome.

questions.stem: What is the difference between an intron and an exon?

options.text: Introns code for proteins; exons do not
Exons are the coding sequences that are expressed; introns are non-coding sequences that are spliced out of the mRNA before translation
Introns are found in prokaryotes; exons are found in eukaryotes
There is no difference — they are the same thing

questions.explanation: Exons are the coding sequences of a gene that are expressed (kept in the mature mRNA). Introns are non-coding sequences that are removed (spliced out) from the pre-mRNA during post-transcriptional modification. Remember: Exons are EXpressed, Introns are INtervening sequences.

questions.stem: What post-transcriptional modifications occur to pre-mRNA in eukaryotes?

options.text: No modifications — mRNA is used directly after transcription
Addition of a 5' cap and poly-A tail, and splicing out of introns
Addition of amino acids to the ends of the mRNA
Conversion of all uracil bases to thymine

questions.explanation: In eukaryotes, pre-mRNA undergoes three main modifications: (1) a 5' cap (modified guanine nucleotide) is added to protect against degradation and aid ribosome binding, (2) a poly-A tail (string of adenine nucleotides) is added to the 3' end for stability, and (3) introns are spliced out, leaving only exons in the mature mRNA.

questions.stem: What is a substitution mutation?

options.text: An extra base is added to the DNA sequence
One base in the DNA sequence is replaced by a different base
A base is removed from the DNA sequence
An entire gene is duplicated

questions.explanation: A substitution (point) mutation is when one base pair in the DNA is replaced by a different base pair. This may change one codon, potentially changing one amino acid in the protein. Due to the degeneracy of the genetic code, some substitutions are 'silent' (the new codon still codes for the same amino acid).

questions.stem: Why are deletion and insertion mutations generally more harmful than substitution mutations?

options.text: They always cause cancer
They cause a frameshift — all codons after the mutation are altered, changing most of the amino acid sequence
They only affect the first amino acid
They are not more harmful — all mutations have the same effect

questions.explanation: Deletion and insertion mutations cause a frameshift — they shift the reading frame of all codons downstream of the mutation. This means every amino acid after the mutation point may be different, usually producing a completely non-functional protein. Substitution mutations only affect one codon, so they tend to be less damaging.

questions.stem: What enzyme catalyses transcription?

options.text: DNA polymerase
DNA helicase
RNA polymerase
Ligase

questions.explanation: RNA polymerase catalyses transcription — it reads the DNA template strand and assembles a complementary mRNA molecule. It binds to the promoter region of the gene and moves along the template strand in the 3' to 5' direction, adding RNA nucleotides in the 5' to 3' direction.

questions.stem: What is the role of DNA ligase in DNA replication?

options.text: To unwind the double helix
To add nucleotides to the growing strand
To join Okazaki fragments together on the lagging strand by forming phosphodiester bonds
To proofread the new strand for errors

questions.explanation: DNA ligase joins the Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand by forming phosphodiester bonds between adjacent nucleotides, creating a continuous strand. The lagging strand is synthesised in short fragments because DNA polymerase can only work in the 5' to 3' direction.

questions.stem: What are the three types of RNA involved in protein synthesis?

options.text: mRNA, tRNA, and rRNA
mRNA, DNA, and ATP
tRNA, rRNA, and dRNA
mRNA, sRNA, and nRNA

questions.explanation: The three types of RNA involved in protein synthesis are: mRNA (messenger RNA, carries the genetic code from DNA to the ribosome), tRNA (transfer RNA, carries amino acids to the ribosome), and rRNA (ribosomal RNA, makes up part of the ribosome structure and has catalytic activity).

questions.stem: How many bases code for one amino acid?
questions.explanation: Three bases (a triplet codon) code for one amino acid. Since there are only 4 different bases, a two-base code would only give 4² = 16 combinations (not enough for 20 amino acids). A three-base code gives 4³ = 64 combinations, which is more than enough, so the code is degenerate.

questions.stem: What is meant by the genetic code being 'universal'?

options.text: All organisms have the same genes
The same codons code for the same amino acids in virtually all organisms
All organisms have the same number of chromosomes
DNA replication occurs the same way in all organisms

questions.explanation: The genetic code is universal because the same codons code for the same amino acids in nearly all living organisms — from bacteria to humans. For example, AUG always codes for methionine (and acts as the start codon). This universality is strong evidence that all life shares a common ancestor.

questions.stem: What is the start codon, and what amino acid does it code for?

options.text: UAA — it codes for alanine
AUG — it codes for methionine
UGA — it codes for glycine
GCA — it codes for tryptophan

questions.explanation: AUG is the start codon and codes for the amino acid methionine. It signals the ribosome to begin translation. UAA, UAG, and UGA are stop codons — they do not code for any amino acid and signal the ribosome to stop translation and release the polypeptide.

questions.stem: What is the difference between the template strand and the coding strand of DNA?

options.text: They are the same strand with two different names
The template strand is read by RNA polymerase during transcription; the coding strand has the same sequence as the mRNA (except T instead of U)
The coding strand is read during transcription; the template strand matches the mRNA
The template strand is only found in prokaryotes; the coding strand is only in eukaryotes

questions.explanation: The template (antisense) strand is the one read by RNA polymerase during transcription (3' to 5'). The coding (sense) strand has the same base sequence as the resulting mRNA (with T in place of U). The mRNA is complementary to the template strand and identical to the coding strand.

questions.stem: What does 'non-overlapping' mean in relation to the genetic code?

options.text: Codons do not share bases — each base is part of only one codon
The same amino acid is never coded for by two different codons
Genes never overlap on a chromosome
The two DNA strands never overlap

questions.explanation: Non-overlapping means each base in the mRNA sequence belongs to one codon only. The codons are read consecutively without any bases being shared between codons. For example, in AUGCCU, AUG is codon 1 and CCU is codon 2 — the bases do not overlap.

questions.stem: What is the difference between DNA and RNA?

options.text: DNA is double-stranded with deoxyribose sugar and thymine; RNA is usually single-stranded with ribose sugar and uracil
DNA is single-stranded; RNA is double-stranded
DNA contains uracil; RNA contains thymine
There are no structural differences between DNA and RNA

questions.explanation: Key differences: DNA is double-stranded, contains deoxyribose sugar, and uses the base thymine (T). RNA is usually single-stranded, contains ribose sugar, and uses uracil (U) instead of thymine. DNA is also typically much longer than RNA molecules.

questions.stem: What is a silent (synonymous) mutation?

options.text: A mutation that kills the cell immediately
A base change that results in a different codon that still codes for the same amino acid, so the protein is unchanged
A mutation that makes no change to the DNA at all
A mutation that only occurs in non-coding DNA

questions.explanation: A silent mutation is a base substitution that changes the codon but still codes for the same amino acid (due to the degeneracy of the genetic code). For example, both GGU and GGC code for glycine. If a mutation changes GGU to GGC, the amino acid sequence is unaffected, so there is no change to the protein.

questions.stem: In which direction does DNA polymerase synthesise a new DNA strand?

options.text: In both directions simultaneously
Direction does not matter in DNA replication

questions.explanation: DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides in the 5' to 3' direction. This means it reads the template strand in the 3' to 5' direction. Because DNA strands are antiparallel, this creates a problem on the lagging strand, which must be synthesised in short Okazaki fragments that are later joined by DNA ligase.
